application.cover_letter_markdown:
Dear hiring team at Kaikuvaara Oy,

For the last few years I've been trying to find my way back to hands-on embedded work. I've been at Meridian Defence Electronics in Oulu since 2007, and the first three years were the ones that defined what I actually want to do with my career. I came in as a junior engineer on the tactical radio product line, and my main task was writing the real-time noise-suppression module for the voice channel in C. The target was a TI TMS320C6748 DSP, the end-to-end latency budget was 4 ms including ADC and DAC overhead, and the algorithm had to fit within 60% of the DSP's cycle budget because the channel equaliser ran on the same core. I converted the floating-point MATLAB prototype to fixed-point, built the frame-based processing pipeline, and spent weeks debugging timing faults through JTAG and Code Composer Studio. That module shipped in 2010 and, as far as I know, it is still in the current production firmware.

After that project my role gradually shifted. Meridian is a small company and the work that needed doing was algorithm design and test automation rather than embedded implementation. I've spent the last decade maintaining the MATLAB simulation environment, designing interference-rejection algorithms for the narrowband voice channel, and building automated regression suites for the audio codec test bench. It's useful work and I'm good at it, but it's not where I want to spend the next decade.

Your senior signal processing engineer role caught my attention because it sits squarely in the embedded, hardware-close domain I've been missing. I am not going to claim that audio DSP for tactical radios and remote-sensing instrument electronics are the same thing — the application domains are clearly different, and I'd have a learning curve on the instrumentation side. What I do think transfers is the discipline of getting code to run correctly on real hardware under real constraints: fixed-point arithmetic, cycle budgets, timing verification, debugging on target. Those problems are portable even when the signals are not.

On the practical side, I have been in Oulu since 2007 and have no intention of leaving. My family is here, my life is here, and the prospect of working on something new without relocating is genuinely what makes this opportunity interesting.

I'd appreciate the chance to talk this through.

Riikka Turunen

To the hiring manager,

The range-compression module I wrote for Vireo's ground-penetrating radar product runs on an ARM Cortex-R5 under an 8 µs deadline per range line — chirp-matched filter, windowing, and overlap-save FFT, all in C, verified to ±0.5 LSB against the MATLAB reference. Three engineers report to me on this track. It started because I'd written most of the firmware and my manager formalised the arrangement six months later. I set sprint scope, review all merge requests, and present the firmware status at the monthly product review. The coordination work turned out to be something I enjoy as well as the technical work, and I'd want to keep developing that side.

On relocation: I currently live in Tampere, but my partner is from Oulu and we've been planning a move there for some time. Your posting made the timeline concrete. My contract has a one-month notice clause, and the move itself is straightforward — we have housing partly arranged through family already.

I'd be glad to discuss this in more detail if it looks like a fit.

Dimitri Muller

application.cover_letter_markdown:
To Kaikuvaara Oy,

Sinikaari Optics does industrial optical inspection — defect detection in sheet steel, paper, plastic film — and I've been their signal processing person since 2005. It's a small company here in Oulu, and I've spent most of my career working on spectral classification and image-correction algorithms for line-scan camera systems. There was a year out in 2007-08 when Sinikaari restructured and my position was cut; I used the time to do a requalification course in industrial automation at Oulujoki UAS, and they brought me back when hiring resumed.

I'm writing about the senior signal processing role at Kaikuvaara because, frankly, after twenty years in the same narrow lane I want a change. The optical inspection domain has been good to me — the problems are real, the engineering is serious — but I've done my version of it. The work you describe, remote-sensing instrument electronics, is a step into a more complex domain that I find genuinely interesting. I've read what I could find about Kaikuvaara's SAR work, and while the signals are different, the underlying problems — making real-time processing chains work against real sensor noise under real constraints — are recognisably the same class of problem I deal with, at a different scale and in a different medium.

I should say something about language, since the posting mentions English as the working language. My entire career at Sinikaari has been conducted in English. The parent company is Swedish, and every design review, technical report, and management presentation is in English. I wrote the user manuals for our last two inspection system releases, presented at the company's annual technical conference in Stockholm on three occasions, and communicate daily in English with engineering colleagues in Linköping. Before Sinikaari, my degree at CRIT was entirely in English.

I'm not going to oversell the domain match. I've done image and spectral signal processing, not radar or payload electronics, and there would be a learning curve. What I bring is two decades of working with real sensor data under production constraints, and the steadiness that comes from having done it for a long time. The sensor types change; the requirement that your algorithm produce correct results on noisy, drifting input does not.

If any of this sounds relevant, I'm available to talk.

Hannu Saarinen

When I moved to Oulu from Gothenburg last year to join Fenno Radar Technologies, I picked this city partly because of the RF and photonics engineering cluster here. Suvanto's Oulu centre, the university's wireless communications research, and the handful of companies doing real radar and signal processing work make it one of the more interesting places in the Nordics for this kind of engineering. It was a side effort within the thesis — not the central contribution — but it gave me a working grounding in estimation theory that I've drawn on since when thinking about tracking problems at Fenno.

As a Danish citizen I have unconditional EU work authorisation. I registered with the Finnish Residency Records Agency when I relocated, and there are no restrictions on my employment.

Finland was a deliberate choice — I moved here for the engineering community, not by accident — and Oulu specifically is where I want to be for the long term.

I also have some experience coordinating technical work in small teams, and I'd welcome the chance to take on more of that in a senior role.

I'd be happy to discuss this further at your convenience.

Andrei Larsen

To the hiring team at Kaikuvaara Oy,

Nordkom Radar Systems has been a good place to work for eleven years, and I'm not leaving because anything is wrong. The maritime radar product line has stabilised, I've maintained the firmware through three hardware revisions, and my scope for growth has reached a ceiling. I want to work somewhere the problems are harder.

My core deliverable at Nordkom is the embedded firmware for the maritime radar's signal processing chain. The current iteration runs on a TI C6678 and processes four receive channels within a 500 µs PRI: range compression via overlap-save FFT, CFAR detection with cell-averaging and ordered-statistic variants, and plot extraction — all in C, all fixed-point. I own the cycle budget and the on-target debugging. When something breaks on a customer installation, I'm the one who gets the call.

I also built and maintain the production test framework in Python — roughly 6,000 lines, 85% pytest coverage, used daily by the production team, CI via GitLab — and I'm responsible for RF front-end calibration: S-parameter sweeps on the R&S ZNB40 and pattern verification in the compact anechoic range. These tasks have become routine, which is honest about where I am and why I'm looking.

The most technically interesting project I've done outside Nordkom was a freelance contract designing an acoustic beamformer for a hearing-aid microphone array. The problem: steer a cardioid beam from a 4-element endfire array toward the wearer's look direction, fed by a head-tracking IMU, on a Cortex-M4F at 64 MHz with a <5 ms latency budget and <10 mW power ceiling. The application domain is nothing like radar, but the underlying work — spatial filtering, interference rejection, calibrating element-to-element gain and phase, making the algorithm fit on a constrained processor — was work I recognised. That project also convinced me I do my best work when the constraints are tight and the resources are small.

What I think I'd bring to Kaikuvaara: the embedded firmware discipline; the production Python tooling; the RF measurement experience; and — from the hearing-aid work — a demonstrated willingness to approach array-processing problems in unfamiliar domains and solve them. What I'd need to learn is the payload-specific context: mission constraints, environmental qualification, and the things that distinguish instrument-grade design from commercial radar. I'd rather state the gap plainly than have it surface after I've started.

On the practical side: I live in Oulu, have done since 2015, and I'm staying. I hold an EU long-term residence permit with unconditional work authorisation. All my professional work has been in English — Nordkom's working language — and my published conference paper (BALSIPCO 2015) and master's thesis from Politecnico del Naviglio are available on request.

I'm available for an interview whenever suits.

Tunde Tanaka

Hello,

Seventeen years in one company is a long time. I joined Tuulikallio Embedded Systems in 2009, straight out of KUT, and I've been doing vibration signal processing ever since — spectral estimation, envelope demodulation, order tracking, all for industrial condition monitoring systems. The work has been technically honest. I've published a conference paper, contributed to an EU research programme, and designed algorithms that run in production across Tuulikallio's installed base. But I have to be frank and say that after nearly two decades the problems have stopped surprising me.

That is really why I'm writing to you. The Senior Signal Processing Engineer role at Kaikuvaara caught my attention because it's a domain I have never worked in — remote-sensing instruments, the kind of electronics that goes into harsh environments and has to work without intervention. At this point in my career I would rather take on something genuinely new than refine algorithms I could write in my sleep. There is a risk in that, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. My background is in vibration and acoustic signal processing, not radar or remote sensing, and there would be a learning curve on more than one front.

What I think I bring is the discipline of working with real sensor data from real hardware, over a long period. I've spent years bridging the gap between MATLAB algorithm models and what the firmware team ships on production hardware — dealing with noise floors, calibration drift, temperature effects, the things that separate a simulation from a working system. The sensor types change; the requirement that your algorithm produce correct results on noisy, drifting, real-world input does not. That experience is not domain-specific. It travels.

I also have the practical advantages of already being here. I've lived in Oulu since 2009, my family is settled, and I have no plans to move. I'm a Finnish permanent resident with full work authorisation. My children were born here, my wife works here, and there's nothing on the logistics side that would complicate a transition.

I'm aware that my vibration-monitoring background may look narrow for this role. But I'd argue that seventeen years of applied signal processing work, including published research and EU collaborative R&D, amounts to something even when the application domain is new. I'm a reasonably fast study when the engineering is real, and I am motivated in a way I haven't been for some time.

Hiroshi Costa

application.cover_letter_markdown:
Dear Kaikuvaara Oy recruitment team,

The thing that drew me into satellite data processing — and the reason I've stayed in this field — is that the data comes from instruments operating under conditions where everything wants to go wrong. Noise is real, calibration drifts are real, and there is no going back to re-measure. You work with what the instrument sends down, and you make it accurate. That aspect of my work at Tuulenkaari Satellite Systems is what I find genuinely compelling, and it's what made your Senior Signal Processing Engineer posting stand out: Kaikuvaara designs the instruments themselves, which is further upstream and, I think, more interesting than what I do on the ground-processing side.

I should be straightforward about the fact that my experience is narrower than what you're probably looking for. My work has been ground-segment data processing — spectral quality assessment, geometric correction, radiometric validation — not the hardware or firmware that generates the signal in the first place. My applied mathematics degree gave me a solid analytical grounding, and at Tuulenkaari I've applied that to real mission data for five years, but I've never designed an instrument or worked on the processing that runs onboard. What I can offer is that time spent handling the output of those systems, and an intimate knowledge of what makes the data good or bad.

I took a year out in 2022-23 to study data engineering through Limmat Institute of Technology Zurich's online programme, partly because I wanted computational skills beyond MATLAB and partly because I needed a break. I came back to Tuulenkaari with a clearer sense of what I wanted next, and that clarity is part of what's driving this application. I want to be closer to the instrument, not just the data it produces.

On the practical side: I currently live in Helsinki, but my wife and I have been considering a move to Oulu for some time. Her company has a branch office there and she has a standing offer to transfer. We visited last autumn and liked the city — the outdoor access especially, since we are both keen cross-country skiers, and the engineering community is smaller and more close-knit than Helsinki's. Relocating for this role would be straightforward and genuinely welcome.

I would be glad to talk about where my background fits and where it doesn't.

Ravi Gupta

The processing pipeline handles 16 receive channels and must complete a full scan's processing within the antenna rotation period.

Designed and implemented the phased-array beamforming engine for Fenno's second-generation maritime radar (2012–2015): frequency-domain beamforming, adaptive null steering for interference rejection, and gain/phase calibration for a 32-element uniform linear array. application.cover_letter_markdown:
My CV tells a straightforward story — twenty-three years at Fenno Radar Technologies in Oulu, all in radar signal processing. What it leaves out are a few things I'd rather explain in person, but this letter will have to do.

On the Python side: in 2019 I rewrote Fenno's offline radar data analysis toolkit from a collection of ad-hoc MATLAB scripts into a structured Python package. It is now about 9,000 lines, used by the entire signal processing group (six engineers) for post-processing recorded radar data, running regression tests against reference scenarios, and generating performance reports. I maintain it, review merge requests from other contributors, and it runs nightly in a Jenkins CI pipeline with roughly 200 test cases. I would not call it glamorous software, but it is tested, documented, version-controlled, and relied upon daily — which is what production means to me.

Regarding my education: my degree is in metallurgical engineering, not electrical engineering or physics. I know this is an unusual background for a signal processing role. What I would point to is twenty-three years of continuous, full-time practice in exactly this field. I have designed phased-array processing chains, embedded DSP firmware, and tracking algorithms, and at this point the distance between my formal education and my working competence has been closed by the work itself. I taught myself the signal processing fundamentals on the job in my first years at Fenno, and the systems I built from that foundation are running in production installations today.

On team leadership: since 2016 I have been the de facto technical lead for the maritime radar signal processing team — four engineers reporting to me, with responsibility for task allocation, design reviews, and integration milestones. I run the weekly technical sync, own the release schedule for the firmware track, and handle technical onboarding for new team members. My formal job title has not changed, which is why it does not appear on the CV, but the responsibility is real and daily.

Working language: Fenno's engineering team operates entirely in English — design documents, code reviews, specifications, customer-facing acceptance-test reports. I have worked in English professionally since 2001 and drafted the company's standard template for customer acceptance-test reports, which is used across all product lines. My education at SIT Bombay was also in English.

I have been in Oulu building radar systems for most of my adult life, and Kaikuvaara's work in remote-sensing instruments is close enough to mine that the transition would be substantive but grounded. I'd welcome the chance to discuss it.

Bartosz Popescu
